To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the phosphorylation‐dependent activation of Spo0F is a result of the phosphorylation‐mediated formation of a network of hydrogen bonds that connect the surface residues involved in protein:protein interactions and the site of phosphoryl group attachment, and that this network is likely to be a general mechanism by which phosphorylated bacterial response regulators activate.

the Spo0F response regulator protein has a phosphorylation‐inducible conformational change, that this conformational change involves the movement of a network of residues, and that the movement of this network of residues is required for Spo0F to interact with the response regulator protein kinase, Spo0B.
the phosphorylation‐dependent activation of Spo0F is mediated through the formation of an intramolecular communication network.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying the molecular mechanisms of protein function, with the goal of understanding the principles of protein design and function.

the identification and characterization of the communication pathways that link the site of phosphorylated residue modification in response regulator proteins to the surface of the protein, and how these pathways are involved in transmitting the phosphorylation‐triggered conformational change to the surface.
understanding the mechanisms that underlie the regulation of signal transduction pathways in bacteria.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the phosphorylated response regulator protein is activated by the formation of an intramolecular communication network that links the site of phosphorylated to regions of the protein that are required for interaction with the cognate sensor protein.
Spo0F is a model for the activation mechanism of all bacterial two‐component response regulators, but not all two‐component response regulator proteins are Spo0F.
the Spo0F protein has a network of communication pathways that link the surface regions involved in protein:protein interactions with the site of phosphoryl transfer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

phosphorylation of the response regulator protein induces a conformational switch in which an α‐helix becomes disordered and the surface of the protein becomes more hydrophilic, and the communication network described here may be the mechanism by which this is accomplished.

the phosphorylation‐dependent conformational change is propagated via a network of communication residues that link the phosphorylation site to the surface region required for interaction with other proteins.
the Spo0F protein is a good model for how bacterial response regulator proteins function.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the communication network is not unique to Spo0F and is likely to be present in all bacterial response regulator domains.
phosphorylation of the receiver domain of Spo0F results in a change in protein conformation that is propagated through the protein, resulting in the activation of the C‐terminal domain.
the phosphorylated response regulator protein is an active conformation, which is poised to interact with other proteins.
